html:
From 1956 the Soviet Union turned the Hungry Steppe, Mirzachoʻl in Uzbek, into one of its biggest cotton growing areas by digging canals from the Syr Darya. The steppe is a dry loess plain of about 10,000 square km on the left bank of the river, between the Fergana Valley and the Kyzylkum desert, mostly in today's Uzbekistan.

Russian engineers had begun irrigating parts of it in the 1880s, and early Soviet plans followed in the 1920s. The big push came under Khrushchev: new canals, state farms, and new towns like Yangiyer and Gulistan for settlers from across the Soviet Union and from Uzbek villages. By the 1970s hundreds of thousands of hectares had been brought under the plough.

It was part of the Soviet drive for cotton that drained the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya and set off the shrinking of the Aral Sea. Poor drainage brought salt to the surface. The cotton economy it built also bred the cotton scandal, and forced labour in the harvest lasted until 2022. Compare the Virgin Lands campaign in Kazakhstan in the same years.
